name: Alexandrite laser hair removal

lead: Alexandrite lasers reduce dark facial and body hair, and clinics commonly use them for fast treatment of large areas on lighter skin tones. The result is visibly less hair growth, a reduction rather than guaranteed total removal.

The 755 nm light is strongly absorbed by melanin, so it heats the hair and follicle while skin cooling protects the surface, damaging actively growing follicles. Alexandrite is among the more studied hair-removal lasers; Wikipedia describes a 2006 review that found roughly 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months across alexandrite, diode and IPL.

paras: Treatment is done in a clinic over multiple sessions spaced weeks apart, because only actively growing hairs respond at any one time. It works best on dark, coarse hair; light, grey, red or fine hair responds poorly. Many people shave beforehand and then maintain with occasional touch-up sessions.

Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, burns and hyper- or hypopigmentation. The FDA defines "permanent" reduction as long-term stable reduction, not guaranteed removal. Tanned or darker skin carries higher pigment-change risk, so patients typically avoid sun exposure around sessions.

Laser hair removal an attractive option for some male patients - Dermatology Times

angle.text: Alexandrite light at 755 nm is absorbed by hair melanin, heating and damaging follicles so dark hair grows back visibly thinner and sparser over sessions. It is used for facial and body hair on lighter skin, and the research base on hair reduction is broad.

lead: Alexandrite laser hair removal uses a 755 nm laser that melanin absorbs strongly, so the light heats dark hair and its follicle and reduces regrowth. For people who want smoother, hair-free skin on the face, neck, body or beard line, or who want to stop shaving, it is one of the standard clinic options, alongside ruby, diode, Nd:YAG and intense pulsed light (IPL).[1][2] The alexandrite wavelength is often chosen for fast treatment of large areas on light to medium skin.[3]

Treatment works by selective photothermolysis: wavelength and pulse length are matched to melanin so the follicle's stem cells are damaged while surrounding skin is spared by cooling.[1] Because only follicles in the growth phase respond, most people need at least eight sessions spaced three to eight weeks apart, sometimes with touch-ups.[1] The American Academy of Dermatology says removing unwanted hair can take six or more sessions and that results are permanent on most body areas, though hormones make results on a woman's face non-permanent.[4] Dark hair against light skin gives the best results; white, light blond, red, grey and fine vellus hair respond poorly.[1][5]

Studies report average hair reductions of roughly 55 to 80 percent depending on skin type and number of sessions, with pigment changes, folliculitis and blistering the main recorded complications.[6][7] Dermatologists also describe the laser as a way to reduce the ingrown hairs and razor bumps that men get along the beard line and neck, because treated hairs become finer and less likely to curl back into the skin.[4][8]
The same alexandrite technology is built into Q-switched and picosecond lasers used for tattoos and pigmented lesions, which are separate treatments.[9][10][11]

paras: Melanin in the hair is the target chromophore. Light absorbed there heats the follicle's basal stem cells, which are destroyed only if the temperature is held for long enough, so pulse duration and fluence (J/cm2) both matter, and spot size changes how deep the energy reaches.[1] Epidermal cooling by contact cooling, cryogen spray or cold air protects the skin and allows higher energy.[1] Treated hairs usually shed over two to three weeks.[1]

Alexandrite's 755 nm wavelength is absorbed by melanin more strongly than Nd:YAG's 1064 nm, which is why it is described as highly effective on dark hair and also more likely to affect pigment in the skin itself.[3][2] A 2005 review lists the ruby (694 nm), alexandrite (755 nm) and diode (810 nm) lasers and IPL as the commonly used devices, with long-pulsed Nd:YAG (1064 nm) described as the safest device for dark-skinned patients.[2]

Hair grows in cycles, and the laser reaches follicles best when the hair is in its active growth phase. That is why treatments are spaced several weeks apart, so that follicles that were resting at one session can be reached at a later one, and why Dermatology Times quotes dermatologists saying that each session typically removes only a share of the hair, with four to seven sessions standard for most body sites.[1][8]

Wikipedia reports that hair-removal lasers were tested experimentally for about 20 years before commercial release in 1995 to 1996, following work by Anderson and Grossman on selective photothermolysis.[1] The FDA cleared the approach in 1997 for 'permanent hair reduction', a phrase defined as long-term stable reduction in the number of hairs regrowing rather than total removal.[1] A 2000 Ankara study found an alexandrite laser faster and less painful than galvanic electrolysis in 12 patients.[1]

A 2005 review noted that ruby, alexandrite, diode and IPL devices all work in light skin (phototypes I to III), producing hair reduction near 75 percent.[2] A 2006 review cited by Wikipedia found no significant short-term difference in efficacy among alexandrite, diode and IPL.[1] In the 2020s, over-the-counter diode devices were cleared for home sale in the United States, according to Wikipedia, expanding the options beyond clinic lasers.[1]

The American Academy of Dermatology lists the armpits, back, bikini area, chest, face (especially the upper lip and chin), legs, neck and shoulders as areas that can be treated.[4] Dermatology Times reports that nearly any hair with pigment can be treated, including hair on the back, where improved technology has cut treatment time from about 90 minutes to 20 to 40 minutes, and that the upper lip takes only a few minutes per session.[5][8]

For men, the beard line, neck, chest and back are commonly discussed areas. A dermatologist quoted by Dermatology Times says laser works 'very elegantly' for pseudofolliculitis barbae, the razor-bump condition more common in men, by making hairs finer and less likely to curl back into the skin.[8] The AAD says more men are seeking laser hair removal and that it can help with razor burn and ingrown hairs; it adds that insurance does not cover the treatment.[4]

Wikipedia cites a 2006 review finding no significant short-term difference between alexandrite, diode and IPL, with about 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months, and side effects reported in 9.5 percent for alexandrite versus 28.9 percent for diode and 15.3 percent for IPL.[1]

A retrospective review of 2,359 patients in Turkey (Fitzpatrick types II to V, 3,830 sites) reported a mean 80.6 percent hair reduction six months after the last treatment, with maximum reductions of 95 percent in the underarm and 92 percent in the bikini area, and complications in 2.2 percent.[6] A trial of 144 people with Asian skin (types III to V) found 32 percent reduction at nine months after one session, 44 percent after two and 55 percent after three, supporting multiple treatments.[7] A study of a 30 mm spot-size handpiece in types II to III reported reduced hair after three to eight sessions at six-week intervals, with mean pain of 4.9 out of 10.[3]

A randomised trial of 48 axillae found hair counts fell by around 80 percent across three sessions regardless of whether treatment fell during menstruation, ovulation or the luteal phase, with pain scores lower later in the series.[12] A study comparing a linear-scanning 808 nm diode laser with a scanned alexandrite laser examined long-term efficacy of the two devices.[13]

Dermatologists quoted in Dermatology Times say the ideal candidate has light skin (Fitzpatrick types I to III) and dark brown or black hair, that multiple treatments are needed, and that light hair is hardest to remove while white hair cannot currently be treated.[5] The 2005 review noted combination radiofrequency-and-light devices and photodynamic therapy under investigation for light hair.[2]

Itching, redness, swelling and perifollicular oedema are usually mild and last two to three days.[1] Acne flare-ups and skin discolouration are the most common serious effects; burns, hypopigmentation, scabbing, purpura and infection are also documented.[1] In the Turkish series the most frequent complications were transient hyperpigmentation (0.7 percent), folliculitis (0.5), transient hypopigmentation (0.5) and blistering (0.4), with no scarring or long-term pigment change.[6] A 1999 paper compared side effects of Q-switched Nd:YAG, long-pulsed ruby and alexandrite lasers.[14]

Wikipedia also records that large-area use of strong topical anaesthetics has caused serious harm and deaths, and that allergic reactions to gels, numbing creams or early shaving can occur.[1] Darker skin carries a higher risk of pigment change, which is why wavelength and cooling are selected by skin type.[2][7] A dermatologist quoted by Dermatology Times says overly aggressive settings can cause hypo- or hyperpigmentation, that modern devices have made this largely a thing of the past, and that surface cooling is critical.[8]

In the United States the FDA regulates the devices, but Wikipedia notes there is no federal licensing for practitioners and rules for operators vary by state.[1] The AAD notes that dermatologists perform the treatment and offers a directory for finding one.[4]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and appearance culture
paras: Laser hair removal is discussed in appearance communities as a way to clear the neck, cheeks, beard line, chest, back or shoulders, to define a beard edge, and to prevent ingrown hairs. Clinics and dermatology press describe growing demand among men, and the AAD says more men than ever are seeking permanent hair reduction.[4][5] In these discussions alexandrite is typically named among clinic wavelengths for lighter skin, with Nd:YAG named for darker skin.[2]

Participants often compare clinic lasers with diode lasers, IPL, electrolysis, waxing and shaving. Electrolysis can remove all hair, including light hair, but is slower; shaving and waxing are temporary.[1][8]

Picosecond and Q-switched alexandrite lasers are studied for tattoos, pigmented lesions such as nevus of Ota, freckles and lentigines, and wrinkles.[9][10][11][15][16][17] A randomised trial of 755 nm laser hair removal for hidradenitis suppurativa found 75 percent clinical response on treated sides versus 33 percent on controls in a small sample.[18] A letter reported that alexandrite hair removal reduced recurrence of pilonidal sinus after surgery, and a case report describes long-pulsed Nd:YAG followed by alexandrite for Becker's nevus, which combines pigment and extra hair.[19][20]

Human studies of alexandrite hair removal include a 2,359-patient retrospective series,[6] a 144-person Asian-skin trial of one, two or three sessions,[7] a randomised menstrual-cycle trial,[12] a study of a large-spot handpiece[3] and a comparison with a linear-scanning 808 nm diode laser.[13] Reviews place alexandrite among devices giving about 75 percent reduction in light skin.[2] Hair-removal side effects of alexandrite and other lasers were compared in 1999.[14] Studies of picosecond alexandrite lasers address tattoos and pigmented lesions,[9][10][15][16][17] and registered trials cover hidradenitis suppurativa, acne scars and skin toning in Asian skin types.[21][22][18][23]

lore.intro: Alexandrite hair removal is discussed in appearance communities mostly as a clinic option for beard-line, neck and body hair; claims about permanence, skin tone and home devices circulate alongside dermatologists' guidance.
